title: Creating 2D sprites - possible to do that free?
author: 0xAriel
selftext:
Hey i've noticed how easy it is to create games and logic using claude or other SOTA models, but when i tried to create sprites, even when based on templates, i found it very hard

I want to create a 2D game, maybe with characters inspired by LittleFighter2 (OG!!!)

But i couldn't find actual options to create art for my game, what do you guys use? ChatGPT \\ Gemini \\ others are just unable to create proper pixel art games, so i wonder if i can get inspirations from you guys here :)

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: Each day you can get one go at an image in ChatGPT, draw a sprite sheet yourself as best as you can, with good spacing, or take your best guess or count pixels. (Lots of free software to do this in). Then pass that image into ChatGPT and request it in both a style you want and what pixel sizes. Not perfect, but often works and is free.

replies.author: 0xAriel
replies.body: Yes this is exactly what i've done, and i used pretty good basic and accurate templates, the results were very inconsistent and negative

comments.author: ffxivthrowaway03
comments.body:
Hows your hardware?

Local generation is the way to go here.  Stable Diffusion for stills, key art, references, etc.  Feed that into an image2video model to make videos of the animations.  Clean up, export frames, cut into a sprite sheet. Import into your engine.

It takes a bit of working at to get yourself a quality pipeline, and there's still a good amount of RNG and curating the best outputs.  But it's a hell of a lot cheaper than paying someone else to do the same exact thing on any one of those fly-by-night sprite generation sites.

replies.author: 0xAriel
replies.body:
doesnt make any sense to use image2video, because i want several sprites and consistency  
I want NORTH\\SOUTH\\EAST\\WEST movement and keep it consistent

My hardware is not great, RTX2070 super, but just theoretically, which SD models would you recommend? something from civitai? because those didnt work out great for me, but perhaps you have a better method than what i tried?

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
several sprites and consistency is specifically why you want image2video.  You make one video of each animation and chop it into a sprite sheet, so the context of the single generation lives through every frame.  You feed it the reference image of your character and prompt it to make a walking video of the character facing East in a consistent end to end loop for 4-8 seconds at maybe 24fps.  Then you slice the video into individual frames, pick out the handful you need for a clean, looped walk animation, and clean up any edges or backgrounds before combining them into a sprite sheet.

Trying to separately generate individual frames is going to give you a slightly different character in every single frame of the animation, hence the single-gen approach of image2video.

Suggesting individual models really depends on the art style of your game, but there's no reason a 2070 with 8GB of VRAM couldn't handle generating the starting character references.  I use Illustrious (SDXL based) for anime-inspired artwork, trained with a custom LORA in my game's style for consistency.  The image2video model actually just got a huge boost with the release of Minimax H3 as open weights, with the one caveat that you cannot use it for production/published assets if you're in select countries (the US being one of them) due to the model's licensing.  There's quantized weights and ComfyUI workflows that reportedly run, albeit slowly, on 8GB VRAM cards but I haven't tried them and can't attest to their quality or prompt adherence.  For the regular weights though, it handled *isometric* NE/SE/NW/SW walk animations in my proof of concept *extremely* well, even recreating totally occluded limbs from the very rough reference images I fed it.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Sprites you can make with stable diffusion locally or use free images from sota models. I wouldn't try making sprite 'sheets' though since it will be nonsensical and largely useless. 

If you're going with pixel art then you need to learn how to process the art to turn it into true pixel art (size it properly, remove mixels, palletize, etc). And then learning how to probably animate the pixel art by hand would be your best bet (assuming small sprites this is pretty dang easy to do and the time it would take you to generate a passable animation cycle is tremendously longer than just getting a tool like aseprite and doing it by hand (again, assuming small sprites. If you're trying high res pixel art  you're in for a rough time regardless.)

You can alternatively look into rigged animation, as there are a number of free tools for that, but it doesn't work well with pixel art. On the plus side, Inverse Kinematics allows for extremely believable physics in 2d and naturally creates transitions or believable changes to your character's pose that you might not be able to account for with standard transition frames.

Regardless of which route you do, be prepared to do a lot of the work yourself if you want it to look polished. AI does not do these things well, regardless of how many gens you have. There is a ton of manual curation involved. I use AI more now than I used to, but I still do 90+% of all character work by hand. But I will go to AI to generate concept art sheets for things like an animation sheet. I can't use it because it's nonsense, but I'll often find a good pose or two and then go into Krita and paint up my character into the pose in question, or if i'm working with a rigged character, I'll go and build out that animation using the reference as a guide. It helps a lot when I don't have a sense for how the type of character might stand (like I know what I WANT it to feel like, but have no idea how that should look until I see it, and then I can propagate it into my own style easy enough.) Seeing as pixel art has zero technical skill demands (a shaky hand isn't going to fuck up your ability to redraw a limb position, for instance) the same could be used to identify key poses and then it's just a matter of manually moving around the pixel art in a way that holds the identity while conveying the movement and shapes you need. Not very time consuming for smaller sprites (For instance an Octopath Traveler sprite would take a minute to  create a new walk frame once you know what you're doing. But something larger like a Street Fighter 3 sprite you'd be better off NOT using pixel art and doing rigged animation if time was a concern, because repositioning that shit for new frames would take a LOT of time.

AI can generate decent character concepts, but keeping the same character, proportions, palette and style across multiple animation frames is still pretty bad. A hybrid workflow with AI for concepts + pixel-art tools for cleanup seems much more realistic right now

comments.author: TheKeplerGambit
comments.body:
You could ask Claude code in your project to spec.what your project needs. Ask it to write a handoff for Claude design.

Then give the handoff to design and work in there. You can give it examples and have it score it's output against those. Iterate until you are happy.

Once happy ask design to package it up and you give the output back to Claude code.

comments.author: AliAlHamwi
comments.body:
The four-direction part is what makes this harder than the thread has credited, and it is worth separating from the animation problem. A model generating each frame independently has no reason to keep your palette, proportions or hood shape stable between them, which is what you saw. A template constrains where things sit on the sheet, not who the character is.

So do it in two passes rather than one. First build the turnaround as four stills, north, south, east and west, and iterate until those four agree with each other. That set is your character, and it is a much easier thing to get right than 32 frames. Then animate each direction separately with the matching still as the reference, so every frame in a cycle is conditioned on the same image. ffxivthrowaway03's image-to-video route works well inside one cycle for exactly that reason, the frames share a single generation's context, but it will not give you the turnaround, because the model has to invent the other three facings.

On tools, Ludo.ai animates an uploaded character image into a sprite sheet of up to 64 frames and exports transparent PNG frames plus a packed sheet with a JSON atlas, with a per-reference setting for whether it passes on the character, the art style, or both: https://ludo.ai I work on it, so weigh that accordingly. Signup credits are enough to try one direction end to end before deciding anything.

The fully hands-off pipeline you asked about does not exist yet at a quality you would ship, and I would not promise you otherwise. What is realistic today is hands-off within a cycle once the reference is locked, with you checking the contact frames.
